title: A novel pathogenic variant in the KCTD7 gene in a patient with neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis (CLN14): a case report and review of the literature
case_prompt:
A previously healthy male infant, born at term after an uneventful pregnancy to first-cousin parents, presented at 9 months of age when his parents noted he could not sit unsupported. By 12 months, he developed sudden jerky movements of his extremities, trunk, and eyes, diagnosed as myoclonus, and exhibited psychomotor regression with loss of sitting, crawling, babbling, and social engagement. Examination showed dysmorphic facial features (low-set ears, up-slanted palpebral fissures, epicanthal folds, depressed nasal bridge), generalized hypotonia, brisk reflexes, and no organomegaly or skin lesions. Initial laboratory tests—including complete blood count, renal and liver function, electrolytes, thyroid function, and plasma lactate—were within normal limits. Noncontrast CT and brain MRI were normal. EEG demonstrated generalized slowing with spikes and slow waves without photic sensitivity. 

At 18 months, he had his first generalized tonic-clonic seizure. Neurologic exam revealed worsening hypotonia and developmental regression. He lost the ability to sit, track objects, and recognize familiar faces, and developed a frequent laugh. Ophthalmologic evaluation showed a hypopigmented fundus with slight temporal disc pallor. Repeat MRI showed mild generalized brain atrophy and white matter disease. Follow-up EEG revealed generalized high-amplitude sharply contoured delta slowing intermixed with theta and alpha activity, with disorganized spikes and sharp waves; photic stimulation was not performed. Despite phenobarbital, levetiracetam, valproate, and clonazepam, generalized seizures and action myoclonus increased in frequency. The clinical presentation suggested neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis among other possibilities, and whole-exome sequencing was requested.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Inborn errors of metabolism — normal metabolic studies argued against a primary metabolic disorder “Initial laboratory tests were within the normal range and included a complete hemogram, renal and liver functions, serum electrolytes, thyroid functions, and plasma lactate levels.”  
2. Leukodystrophy — lack of characteristic demyelinating changes on imaging made leukodystrophy unlikely “A non-contrast brain CT scan and a brain MRI were ordered, and they returned as normal … A follow-up brain MRI indicated evidence of mild generalized brain atrophy and white matter disease.”  
3. Mitochondrial cytopathies — absence of lactic acidosis and normal lactate levels decreased the likelihood of a mitochondrial disorder “Initial laboratory tests … plasma lactate levels … were within the normal range.”  
4. Progressive myoclonic epilepsy (PME) — distinguished from CLN14 by the absence of vision loss and brain atrophy in PME, whereas our patient had both features “Clinically, PME and CLN14 are distinguished by the earlier onset, more rapid progression, accompanying visual loss, progressive brain atrophy, and early death seen in CLN14.”  
5. Neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis (NCL) — the combination of regression, refractory myoclonus, vision impairment, and brain atrophy suggested NCL and prompted genetic testing “The clinical presentation suggested NCL as a possible diagnosis among other differential conditions, such as inborn errors of metabolism, leukodystrophy, and mitochondrial cytopathies.”
